verdict: Avoid new fruit and vegetable processing exposure in Parwanoo until power reliability and local demand stabilise; only selective, tightly-structured lending to working-capital-light processors with confirmed offtake.
title: Parwanoo Fruit & Vegetable Processing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Parwanoo processor buys seasonal fruit and vegetables, converts them into pulp, frozen or snack lines, and sells into domestic and export markets.** Cash is locked in the crop window: you pay growers at harvest, hold inventory through processing, then wait on buyer credit. **The value sits in the processing line and the offtake contract, not in the raw material, which is perishable and price-volatile.** ICRA flags that raw material is the largest cost and that agro-climatic variation hits both availability and pricing [8][9]. So when a proposal lands, check the crop calendar against the drawing-power cycle; if the buyer credit period runs past the next harvest, ask how the gap is funded.

## Where cash and value actually sit
**Capex is heavy and lumpy — cold storage, freezing, retort lines — while margins are thin and set by the buyer.** The peer, Foods & Inns, shows the pattern: Q4 profit fell 16% from ₹23 crore to ₹19 crore on lower volumes even as margin improved to 6.6% from 5.8% [4]. **Realisation, not volume, is the swing factor** — the same peer saw realisations decline 25.3% [4]. So when a proposal lands, check realisation trend per unit, not just tonnage; if realisations are falling while volumes rise, ask for the buyer-wise price list.

## What has broken now
**Parwanoo's core advantage — cheap, reliable power — is gone.** The state sold 600 MW to Kerala, and the Parwanoo Industry Association reports unscheduled load shedding, low voltage and fluctuations, with effective shortage now 20% [1]. **Continuous-process lines lose product on every trip**, and investors must add transformer, stabiliser and UPS, raising cost of production [1]. This is local news from October 2026 and it is current. The data pack confirms the stress: Himachal GST collections -22.8% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1%, and electricity demand -6.8% versus India +9.5% [D]. **The data-based call is AVOID (score 24).**

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue processors with captive or contracted power, frozen and snack lines with confirmed domestic offtake, and units tied to institutional buyers.** The peer's frozen food volume grew about 39% year-over-year in Q2 FY26 [6], and snacks and pulp are showing growth with capacity expansion underway [7]. **Avoid units dependent on grid power for continuous lines, single-buyer exporters, and anyone without a power backup plan.** Structure as working-capital limits against confirmed orders, with a cash-flow sweep and monthly stock statements. Take monthly: power-backup status, order book, buyer-wise receivables ageing, and stock-and-receivables position.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch power tripping frequency and the unit's own backup adequacy first** — that is the live risk in Parwanoo [1]. **Then watch realisation per unit and buyer concentration** — the peer's 25.3% realisation decline [4] is the template. **Finally watch the crop-to-cash gap**: if inventory days stretch past the next harvest without a matching order, the unit is funding seasonality with debt. Note that sources say little specifically about Parwanoo's processing units beyond the power story; the rest is first principles and peer evidence.
watch: Power backup status and load-shedding log (monthly)
Any unit without full backup -> reduce limit or seek additional collateral
Realisation per unit and buyer-wise price list (monthly)
Falling realisation with rising volumes -> ask for buyer contracts and reprice risk
Inventory days past next harvest without matching order -> stop fresh drawdown
Single buyer above half of sales -> seek diversification plan or guarantee
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
